slide.heading: Muscle & Bone
slide.subheading: How muscles contract, and how bone is always being rebuilt

lines.text: Good morning. I'm Kwame Asante, physiology. Wednesday you meet the muscles in the lab; today, how they work.
Every movement starts with an action potential and ends with two proteins sliding past each other. Calcium is the switch.
And in the second half: bone, which looks inert but is being torn down and rebuilt all your life.

slide.heading: From action potential to calcium
bullets: ACh at the neuromuscular junction: end-plate potential
Action potential runs down the T-tubules
DHP receptor (voltage sensor) pulls open RyR1
Ca²⁺ floods out of the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Ca²⁺ binds troponin C; tropomyosin moves

nodes.label: RyR1 opens: Ca²⁺ out of SR

lines.text: At the neuromuscular junction, acetylcholine opens nicotinic receptors and the muscle fiber fires an action potential.

It dives into the fiber along the T-tubules. There, in skeletal muscle, a voltage sensor, the dihydropyridine receptor, is physically linked to the ryanodine receptor in the sarcoplasmic reticulum, and pulls it open.
Calcium pours out, binds troponin C, and tropomyosin rolls off the myosin-binding sites on actin.
A rare mutation in the ryanodine receptor makes it open in response to certain anesthetics. The result is malignant hyperthermia, and you should know its antidote.

slide.heading: The cross-bridge cycle
bullets: Myosin head binds actin
Power stroke as phosphate is released
ATP binds: myosin lets go of actin
ATP hydrolysis re-cocks the head
No ATP: rigor

lines.text: With the sites exposed, a cocked myosin head binds actin and releases its phosphate: the power stroke pulls the filament along.
Here's the counterintuitive part. It takes a new ATP molecule to make myosin let go.
Hydrolyzing it re-cocks the head for the next stroke. So when ATP runs out after death, the heads stay stuck: rigor mortis.

slide.heading: Motor units and force
bullets: A motor unit: one motor neuron and its fibers
Size principle: small units are recruited first
Faster firing: summation, then tetanus
Type I: slow, oxidative, fatigue-resistant
Type II: fast, glycolytic, powerful, fatigable

lines.text: How do you pick up an egg without crushing it? You grade force two ways.
One motor neuron and all the fibers it supplies are a motor unit. As effort rises you recruit more units, small ones first and big ones last. That's the size principle.
You also fire each unit faster, so the twitches summate into a smooth tetanus.
Postural muscles are rich in slow, oxidative type I fibers; a sprinter's are rich in fast type II.

slide.heading: Bone is always being rebuilt
bullets: Osteoblasts lay down osteoid, then mineralize it
Osteoclasts resorb bone (from the macrophage line)
RANKL on osteoblasts activates RANK on osteoclasts
Osteoprotegerin (OPG) is a decoy for RANKL
PTH and vitamin D tune the balance

lines.text: Your skeleton is replaced about every ten years. Two cells do the work.
Osteoblasts build: they lay down osteoid and mineralize it. Osteoclasts, big multinucleated cells from the macrophage line, dissolve it.
They talk to each other. Osteoblasts display RANKL, which binds RANK on osteoclast precursors and makes them mature. Osteoprotegerin is a decoy that soaks up RANKL.
Parathyroid hormone and vitamin D tune the balance, to keep the blood calcium steady.

slide.heading: Osteoporosis
bullets: Too little bone, poorly organized: fractures
Estrogen loss after menopause speeds resorption
DEXA T-score ≤ −2.5
Bisphosphonates: bind bone, poison osteoclasts
Take upright with water; rare jaw necrosis

lines.text: When resorption outruns formation for years, you get osteoporosis: fragile bones and fractures of the hip, spine and wrist.
Estrogen restrains osteoclasts, so bone loss speeds up after menopause.
We diagnose it with a DEXA scan: a T-score of minus two and a half or below.
The first-line drugs are bisphosphonates. They bind to bone and are taken up by osteoclasts, which then die.

slide.heading: Summary
bullets: Ca²⁺ from the SR, via RyR1, binds troponin C
ATP is needed to release myosin
Recruit small motor units first
RANKL drives osteoclasts; bisphosphonates stop them

lines.text: To sum up: calcium switches contraction on, ATP lets go, and bone is a balance between the osteoblast and the osteoclast.
This afternoon, the anatomy lab: the muscles of the arm and the axilla. Bring your atlas.
